doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Winning the Buffalo State job in 1976
summary: After another candidate failed to show, he was offered a two-year contract on Tallmadge's advice and later team-taught with him.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: pretty well. So I had the job pretty much, and then I’ll never forget, I got a call over at Cole’s. And there was one more guy they had to interview. And Tallmadge, he goes, “Chuck, I’ve got to tell you, this crazy guy came in from New York City, his name is Brown, he’s written two books, he has a doctorate, you only have a master’s, and I know you’re working on” — I finished the second master’s in film theory with Jerry O’Grady over at Media Studies. And I did a lot of things on music, film music and blah, blah, blah. He said, “I told them, we haven’t seen this guy teach. Let him teach a class to us.” “No, no, we want him. He’s got all the ingredients.” So I didn’t get the job. So I go back to Baker Hall. And it turns out I get a call, Peter Yates was still there by the way, hanging by a thread. And now it’s the second week of school and Jerry Close comes over and we’re going to run around the track at Buff State, and we’re getting ready for basketball you know. And he says, “Oh by the way, you got a call from a professor at Buff State.” I said, “Okay, I’ll look at it, let’s do the run.” Now it had already been two and a half weeks teaching in the City of Buffalo. I’d leave Baker Hall, I thought I’d try something different, with Ex Ed. I met with the families and they loved me and I loved them. It was a nice situation. And Peter Yates goes, “Well we have to tell you something, Charles.” This guy Brown, you know we’re over here on Elmwood Avenue in the Albright Building, and he’s teaching where I was teaching. None of those people ever came over there, because it was too far in a round building. He hadn’t been there for two and a half weeks. We don’t know if some angel of a secretary didn’t send him the contract, or he just took another job and thought they were jerks, he never showed up. He says, “We’re in a bind.” Now Bill is in Berea, Kentucky, where he had a chair at a school for mountain children where Bradley Kincaid went and had a great collection of the Carter family. I called him up, I says, “They offered me the job, but they only offered me one year. I’m making sixteen and they’re offering me twelve.” And I was making eighteen and they were offering me twelve. This was back in 1976. He says, “Don’t worry about the money, you’ll make it up, but don’t take a one year contract. They’ll be interviewing for your job while you’re teaching.” So I tried to get a three-year and they only gave me a two-year. He says, “That’s okay, they will not — you’ve got it down.” Because I’d been teaching all those summers and night classes with him. I team taught with him for five years as well, until he left. And sure enough I got the job. And every summer Bill would come, Bill would come to visit me for four, five days, and stay with his son, and I’d have him tell the story about how this guy tried to fire him when he wanted to teach this music.
That’s great. Well let me follow-up on this.
I’m sorry. I’m very long-winded. © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
